text: According to the lesson, what does food provide your body?
solution: Food provides the energy your body needs to grow, repair itself, maintain body temperature, and move. Flavor is a bonus, not the reason food matters.
hint: Think about what lets you run, heal, and grow.

text: Which list matches the four ways the lesson says your body uses food energy?
answers: Grow, repair itself, maintain body temperature, and move
Grow, make sunlight, breathe water, and sleep
Move, make oxygen, absorb sunlight, and shrink
Repair itself, make soil, make sugar, and glow
solution: The lesson names four jobs: growing, repairing itself, maintaining body temperature, and moving. Making sugar from sunlight is what producers do, not people.
hint: Pick the list where every job is something a human body really does.

text: You scrape your knee and it heals over a week. Which use of food energy is that?
solution: Healing a scrape is your body repairing itself, and repair takes energy from food.
hint: What is the body doing to the damaged skin?

text: On a freezing morning, your body stays warm inside. Which use of food energy helps?
answers: Getting energy straight from the Sun
solution: Keeping your body warm is maintaining body temperature, one of the four uses of food energy in the lesson.
hint: Which job is about staying warm?

text: A fifth grader is two inches taller than last year. Which use of food energy does this show?
solution: Getting taller is growth. The lesson says food gives your body energy to grow.
hint: What changed about the student’s size?

text: Running laps at recess uses food energy for which job?
solution: Running is movement. Your muscles use energy from food to move.
hint: What is your body doing during a lap?

text: Maya says, “Food is only for taste. If I liked plain food, I wouldn’t need to eat.” What is the best response?
answers: Food gives the body energy to grow, repair, stay warm, and move, whatever it tastes like
She is right; taste is the only reason to eat
Food is only needed for moving, not for growing
Only adults need energy from food
solution: Taste is enjoyable, but the lesson explains that food provides energy for growing, repairing, maintaining body temperature, and moving.
hint: Ask what food does for the body, not how it tastes.

text: Bacon and eggs, a hamburger, and jambalaya are very different meals. What do they have in common?
answers: Each one provides food energy for your body
Each one makes its own food from sunlight
Each one has no energy until it is cooked
solution: Every meal in the lesson gives your body food energy. Cooking changes food but is not where food energy comes from.
hint: Think about why the lesson mentions these meals.

text: Why would someone who went without enough food for a long time have trouble growing and healing?
answers: Their body would not get enough energy for growth and repair
Their body would make food from sunlight instead
Skipping food gives the body extra energy
Growing and healing do not use any energy
solution: Growing and repairing both use energy, and that energy comes from food. Without enough food, the body cannot do these jobs well.
hint: Connect growing and healing to what food supplies.

text: Which activity is NOT one of the lesson’s four uses of food energy in your body?
solution: Healing, walking, and staying warm match repair, movement, and body temperature. People cannot turn sunlight into sugar; producers do that.
hint: Three choices are things your body does. Find the one only producers do.

text: Where does all the food energy that passes between organisms first come from?
solution: The lesson says all the food energy that passes between organisms comes from the Sun.
hint: Trace the energy back to the very beginning.

text: How does the Sun’s energy first get into a food chain?
answers: Plants use sunlight to make their own food
Animals soak up sunlight through their fur
Mushrooms collect sunlight from dead logs
Rain carries sunlight into the soil
solution: Plants and other producers use sunlight to make their own food. That energy passes to other organisms when they eat the plants.
hint: Which organisms can make their own food?

text: A grasshopper eats grass. Where did the energy in the grass originally come from?
answers: Sunlight the grass used to make food
The mouse that eats the grasshopper
The bugs living in the soil
solution: Grass uses sunlight to make food. The grasshopper gets that energy by eating the grass.
hint: Ask how the grass got its energy before anything ate it.

text: Which statement about energy in a food chain is true?
answers: It starts with sunlight captured by plants and passes to eaters
It starts with the top predator and moves down to plants
It starts in decomposers and moves to plants
Each animal makes its own energy from nothing
solution: Energy enters when plants use sunlight to make food. It passes along when organisms eat one another.
hint: Where does the chain begin, and which way does energy go?

text: Your hamburger bun is made from wheat. Which path shows how the bun’s energy reached you?
solution: The wheat plant used sunlight to make food, and you got that energy by eating the bun.
hint: Start with the original energy source and end with the eater.

text: What happens to energy when an animal eats a plant?
answers: Energy stored in the plant passes to the animal
The plant’s energy goes back to the Sun
solution: When an animal eats a plant, energy the plant made using sunlight passes to the animal.
hint: Think about what the animal gains by eating.

text: If sunlight stopped reaching a meadow for a long time, what would happen first?
answers: Grass could not make food, so less energy would enter the food chain
Mice would start making their own food
solution: Grass needs sunlight to make food. Without it, less energy enters the chain, and every eater depends on that energy.
hint: Which organism uses sunlight directly?

text: Jambalaya has rice, shrimp, and sausage. Where did all the food energy in it begin?
solution: The stove heats the food, but the food energy began as sunlight captured by producers. Rice is a plant, and the shrimp and sausage came from animals that ate producers or other consumers.
hint: Cooking makes food hot. Where did the food energy itself come from?

text: Leo says, “Animals that eat only meat don’t depend on the Sun.” What is wrong with that claim?
answers: The animals they eat got energy from plants, which used sunlight
Nothing; meat-eaters are separate from the Sun
Only decomposers depend on the Sun
solution: A hawk eats a snake, the snake ate a mouse, and the mouse ate a grasshopper that ate grass. The grass captured the sunlight, so the hawk’s energy still came from the Sun.
hint: Follow the meat back through each thing that was eaten.

text: Which word best describes the Sun’s role in every food chain in this lesson?
solution: The Sun is not an organism in the chain. It is the original source of the energy that producers capture.
hint: The Sun does not eat anything. What does it provide?

text: In the class roundtable, students said all food chains and webs get energy from the Sun. Which evidence supports that?
answers: Grass uses sunlight to make food
Animals warm up in the sunshine
solution: Producers such as grass use sunlight to make food, and every other organism gets energy by eating producers or animals that ate them.
hint: Which choice shows sunlight becoming food?

text: The graphic organizer draws arrows from the Sun to an oak tree, grass, and algae. What do those arrows show?
answers: Each producer gets its energy from the Sun
The plants give their energy to the Sun
solution: The organizer says plants get energy from the Sun. The arrows point from the Sun to each producer because energy flows that way.
hint: Arrows follow the energy.

text: What is a food chain?
answers: The movement of food energy from one organism to another
A list of foods a person likes best
A row of plants growing in a garden
A chain that holds a nest together
solution: The lesson defines a food chain as the movement of food energy from one organism to another.
hint: Think about what moves along the chain.

text: Which food chain from the lesson is in the correct order?
solution: Grass makes food from sunlight, a grasshopper eats the grass, a mouse eats the grasshopper, a snake eats the mouse, and the hawk eats the snake.
hint: Start with the producer, then follow who eats whom.

text: In the lesson’s food chain, what does the mouse eat?
solution: In grass → grasshopper → mouse → snake → hawk, the mouse gets energy by eating the grasshopper.
hint: Look at the link just before the mouse.

text: What eats the snake in the lesson’s food chain?
solution: The hawk eats the snake for energy. It is the last animal in the chain.
hint: Look at the link just after the snake.

text: Which organism starts the lesson’s food chain?
solution: Grass starts the chain because it uses sunlight to make its own food.
hint: Which one does not eat anything?

text: In the lesson’s grass-to-hawk example, what job do the mushrooms do?
answers: They break down dead materials left behind
They are eaten by the grass
They give sunlight to the grass
solution: The lesson says any dead materials left behind are broken down by the mushrooms.
hint: What happens to dead organisms in the example?

text: Which of these food chains starts correctly?
solution: A food chain starts with a producer. Lettuce makes food from sunlight, a rabbit eats lettuce, and a fox eats the rabbit.
hint: Find the chain that starts with a plant.

text: In a pond, small fish eat pond plants and herons eat small fish. Which food chain is correct?
solution: Energy goes from the pond plants (the producer) to the small fish that eat them, then to the heron.
hint: Put the producer first, then each eater in order.

text: If all the mice disappeared from grass → grasshopper → mouse → snake → hawk, which organism would lose its food in that chain?
solution: In this chain, the snake gets energy by eating the mouse. Without mice, the snake loses that food. In a real food web it might eat something else.
hint: Which organism eats the mouse?

text: In grass → grasshopper → mouse → snake → hawk, which organism gets energy that has passed through the most links?
solution: The Sun’s energy goes into the grass, then the grasshopper, the mouse, and the snake before it reaches the hawk at the end.
hint: Count the steps from the start of the chain.

text: Which food chain from the graphic organizer is in the correct order?
solution: The oak tree is the producer, the squirrel eats from the oak tree, and the eagle eats the squirrel.
hint: Start with the producer.

text: On the graphic organizer’s pond chain, which organism eats the minnows?
solution: The organizer’s chain is algae → minnows → bass, so the bass eats the minnows.
hint: Look at the link right after the minnows.

text: In grass → cow → humans, what role do the humans play?
answers: Consumers that get energy by eating the cow
Producers that make food from sunlight
Decomposers that break down dead grass
The energy source for the chain
solution: Humans are at the end of this chain. They are consumers who get energy by eating the cow, which got energy from the grass.
hint: Do humans make food or eat it?

text: In a food chain diagram, what do the arrows show?
answers: How energy is passed from one organism to another
solution: The lesson says the arrows show how energy is passed from one organism to the next.
hint: The arrows follow something that moves when organisms eat.

text: Which way should the arrow point between grass and a grasshopper?
answers: From the grass to the grasshopper
From the grasshopper to the grass
No arrow; they are not connected
solution: The grasshopper eats the grass, so energy moves from the grass to the grasshopper. The arrow points toward the eater.
hint: Which way does the energy travel when the grasshopper eats?

text: In “mouse → snake,” what does the arrow mean?
answers: Energy moves from the mouse to the snake when the snake eats it
The mouse turns into a snake
The snake gives energy to the mouse
solution: An arrow points from the food to the eater. Here the snake eats the mouse and gets its energy.
hint: The arrow points toward the organism that gets the energy.

text: Kai drew “hawk → snake” to show that the hawk eats the snake. How should he fix it?
answers: Point the arrow from the snake to the hawk
Leave it; arrows point from the eater to the food
Remove the arrow because hawks are not in food chains
Point the arrow from the hawk to the Sun
solution: Energy flows from the snake to the hawk when the hawk eats it, so the arrow should be “snake → hawk.”
hint: Arrows follow the energy, not the hunter.

text: In the lesson’s diagram, many arrows point to the mushrooms. What does that show?
answers: Energy from many dead organisms ends up with the mushrooms
Mushrooms give energy to all the animals
Mushrooms are where the food chain begins
solution: Mushrooms break down dead materials from the grass and from every animal, so arrows from all of them point to the mushrooms.
hint: What do mushrooms do with dead materials?

text: An arrow points from a deer to a mountain lion. Which statement is correct?
answers: The mountain lion eats the deer and gets its energy
The deer eats the mountain lion
The deer makes food for the mountain lion from sunlight
solution: The arrow points from the food to the eater, so the mountain lion eats the deer.
hint: Which organism does the arrow point toward?

text: Which arrow is drawn correctly?
solution: Energy flows from food to eater. The grasshopper eats grass, so “grass → grasshopper” is correct. The others point backward.
hint: For each choice, ask which one is doing the eating.

text: A good way to read an arrow in a food chain is...
solution: “Grass → grasshopper” reads “grass is eaten by the grasshopper” or “grass gives energy to the grasshopper.”
hint: Try reading “grass → grasshopper” out loud with each choice.

text: In the diagram, an arrow goes from the grass straight to the mushrooms. What could this show?
answers: Mushrooms break down dead grass and get its energy
solution: Mushrooms are decomposers. When grass dies, they break it down and get its energy, so the arrow points from the grass to the mushrooms.
hint: Remember what mushrooms do with dead materials.

text: How many arrows does it take to connect grass → grasshopper → mouse → snake → hawk as one chain?
solution: Five organisms have four connections between them: grass to grasshopper, grasshopper to mouse, mouse to snake, and snake to hawk.
hint: Count the gaps between the organisms, not the organisms.

text: Students said energy in a food chain flows “like a one-way street.” What does that mean?
answers: Energy moves from the food to the eater, not back
Energy goes back and forth between eater and food
Energy can only move along roads
Energy moves from the hawk back to the grass
solution: When an organism gets eaten, its energy moves to the eater. It does not flow back, so the arrows all go one way.
hint: Which way does energy go when something is eaten?

text: On the Stringy Connections class food web, what do the arrows show?
answers: The flow of energy from one organism to another
solution: The worksheet asks students to use arrows to show the flow of energy from one organism to another.
hint: Read the directions for drawing the class food web.

text: What is a food web?
answers: A group of overlapping or connected food chains
A spider’s web for catching food
A list of only the plants in an area
solution: The lesson defines a food web as a group of overlapping or connected food chains.
hint: A web is made of many strands joined together.

text: Why do food chains in an environment cross each other?
answers: Organisms eat more than one thing, so they belong to many food chains
Every animal eats exactly one food
Plants move from one chain to another
The Sun connects only to hawks
solution: Just as you eat more than one food, organisms eat more than one thing. That puts them in several food chains, and the chains cross.
hint: Think about how many kinds of food one animal eats.

text: The lesson compares food webs to a school lunch tray. What idea does the tray show?
answers: Like you, organisms eat more than one kind of food
Organisms eat only one food at a time
Food webs include only human food
solution: A lunch tray holds many foods. Organisms also eat more than one thing, which links many food chains into a web.
hint: What do you notice about how many foods are on the tray?

text: Which statement about the size of a food web matches the lesson?
answers: A food web can be big or small
A food web must have exactly five organisms
A food web is always bigger than an ocean
A food web includes only animals
solution: The lesson says a food web can be big or small, with many kinds of plants and animals or just a few.
hint: Does the lesson set a required number of organisms?

text: Big or small, the organisms in a food web fall into which two categories?
solution: The lesson says every organism in a food web is either a producer or a consumer. Decomposers are a special group of consumers.
hint: One category makes food; the other eats it.

text: A snake eats mice and also eats frogs. What does this mean in a food web?
answers: The snake is part of more than one food chain
The snake can only be in one food chain
The snake no longer needs energy
solution: Because the snake eats two kinds of animals, it belongs to at least two food chains. Those chains connect at the snake.
hint: How many different food chains lead to the snake?

text: Which best describes the difference between a food chain and a food web?
answers: A chain is one path of energy; a web is many connected paths
A chain has more organisms than a web
A web has only plants; a chain has only animals
They mean exactly the same thing
solution: A food chain shows one path of energy. A food web shows many chains that overlap and connect.
hint: Picture one line compared with a net of lines.

text: Owls and snakes both eat mice. How does this connect food chains?
answers: The mouse links a chain to the owl with a chain to the snake
Mice make food for owls from sunlight
It removes the mouse from the web
solution: The mouse is eaten by two different consumers, so it is a crossing point where two food chains meet.
hint: Find the organism both chains share.

text: Why can a food web show more about an environment than one food chain?
answers: It shows that most organisms eat, and are eaten by, more than one kind of organism
It shows only the biggest animal
It shows that energy comes from the soil
solution: A single chain shows one path. A web shows the many feeding connections that really exist, because organisms eat more than one thing.
hint: What does a web include that one chain leaves out?

text: In a meadow, grasshoppers eat grass and rabbits also eat grass. What do these two food chains share?
answers: Grass, the producer at the start of both
A hawk at the start of both
A decomposer as the first link
solution: Both chains start with grass. Shared organisms like this are where food chains connect into a web.
hint: Which organism shows up in both chains?

text: The comparison diagram says food chains are “direct.” What does that mean?
answers: A chain shows one thing eating another in a single path
A chain shows many paths crossing
A chain shows energy flowing backward
solution: A food chain is one straight path: one thing eats another. A food web is a bunch of food chains together.
hint: Picture one line instead of a net.

text: According to the comparison diagram, which is true of both food chains and food webs?
answers: Both show producers, consumers, and energy moving
Both show energy moving from eaters back to the Sun
solution: The overlap in the diagram says chains and webs both have plants and animals, both show consumers and producers, and both show energy moving.
hint: Look at the part where the two shapes overlap.

text: What is a producer?
answers: An organism that gets its energy directly from the Sun
An organism that eats only animals
An organism that breaks down dead things
An animal that hunts at night
solution: The lesson says producers are organisms that get their energy directly from the Sun by turning sunlight into food.
hint: Producers make, or “produce,” their own food.

text: Which of these is a producer?
solution: Lettuce turns sunlight into food, so it is a producer. Eagles and deer are consumers, and mushrooms are decomposers.
hint: Which one makes its own food from sunlight?

text: You eat a lettuce salad. According to the lesson, what have you eaten?
solution: The lesson says that if you have eaten lettuce or another vegetable, you have eaten a producer.
hint: Lettuce is a plant that makes its own food.

text: How does the lettuce plant help your body?
answers: It changes sunlight into food your body uses as fuel
It gives your body sunlight directly
It decomposes the food in your stomach
It eats other organisms for you
solution: Lettuce changes sunlight into food. When you eat it, your body uses that food as fuel.
hint: Follow the energy from the Sun to the lettuce to you.

text: Why does the lesson say producers are very important to life on Earth?
answers: Without them, other organisms would not survive
They eat all of the consumers
They break down every dead animal
solution: Producers bring the Sun’s energy into food webs. Other organisms get energy by eating them, so without producers they could not survive.
hint: Ask where every consumer’s energy starts.

text: A garden has rows of lettuce, onions, and cabbage. What do these plants have in common?
answers: They are producers that make food from sunlight
They are consumers that eat insects
They get energy by eating the soil
solution: Garden vegetables are plants, and plants are producers that use sunlight to make food.
hint: Are these organisms making food or eating it?

text: Ava says, “Plants get their food by eating the soil.” Which correction matches the lesson?
answers: Plants are producers that make their own food using sunlight
Plants eat dead animals for food
Plants get food only from fertilizer
solution: Producers make food by combining carbon dioxide and water using sunlight. They do not eat soil.
hint: How does the lesson say producers get energy?

text: Which organism in grass → grasshopper → mouse → snake → hawk is the producer?
solution: Grass is the only organism in the chain that uses sunlight to make its own food.
hint: Which one does not need to eat?

text: Which sentence best explains why producers come first in food chains?
answers: They capture energy from the Sun, and other organisms get energy by eating them
They are always the smallest organisms
They eat the animals after them in the chain
They are the last to receive energy
solution: Food chains follow energy. Producers bring it in from the Sun, and every other link gets energy by eating.
hint: Where does the energy enter the chain?

text: If a disease killed all the grass in a field, what would the lesson’s ideas predict?
answers: Grasshoppers and the animals that depend on them would lose food energy
Nothing would change for the animals
Mice would start making food from sunlight
solution: Grass is the producer. Without it, grasshoppers lose food, and so do the mice, snakes, and hawks that depend on them.
hint: Follow the chain from the producer to every eater.

text: The graphic organizer says all food webs begin with...
solution: The organizer says all food webs begin with plants, which are called producers because they make their own food.
hint: What makes its own food?

text: Which list contains only producers from the class food web?
answers: Cattails, dandelions, red alpine campion, and oak tree
solution: The class listed cattails, dandelions, red alpine campion, and the oak tree as producers. They are plants that make food using the Sun’s energy.
hint: Find the list made of plants.

text: Algae starts one of the graphic organizer’s food chains. Why does it belong at the start?
answers: It makes its own food using the Sun’s energy, like a plant
solution: Algae is placed in the producer spot because it uses the Sun’s energy to make its own food. Minnows eat it, and bass eat the minnows.
hint: What do all the organisms in the first boxes have in common?

text: Producers combine carbon dioxide, water, and sunlight to make which two things?
solution: The lesson says producers combine carbon dioxide from the air with water and sunlight to produce oxygen and sugar.
hint: Name the two things that are made, not the ingredients.

text: Where does a producer get the carbon dioxide it uses to make food?
solution: The lesson says producers take carbon dioxide from the air.
hint: The lesson names where carbon dioxide comes from.

text: Which of these is an ingredient producers use to make food?
solution: Water and carbon dioxide go in, along with sunlight. Oxygen and sugar come out. Producers do not use meat.
hint: Ingredients go in; products come out.

text: Which of these does a producer make?
solution: Producers make sugar and oxygen. Carbon dioxide, water, and sunlight are what they start with.
hint: Choose something that comes out of the process.

text: What does sunlight provide when a producer makes food?
solution: Sunlight supplies the energy. The materials are carbon dioxide from the air and water.
hint: Which choice is energy rather than a material?

text: The lesson says producers turn sunlight into food through what kind of process?
solution: Producers turn sunlight into food through a chemical process: carbon dioxide and water change into sugar and oxygen.
hint: New substances are made during this process.

text: Which model best shows how a producer makes food?
answers: Carbon dioxide + water + sunlight → sugar + oxygen
solution: Ingredients go on the left of the arrow and products on the right: carbon dioxide, water, and sunlight make sugar and oxygen.
hint: Check that the ingredients and products match the lesson.

text: A plant is kept in a dark closet for weeks. Why would it struggle to make food?
answers: It lacks the sunlight needed to make sugar
solution: Producers need sunlight to make sugar. Without light, the plant cannot make food, even with water and air.
hint: Which ingredient from the lesson is missing in a dark closet?

text: Jordan says, “Plants take in oxygen and sugar to make carbon dioxide.” What is wrong?
answers: He has it backward: plants use carbon dioxide and water to make sugar and oxygen
Plants use soil to make sunlight
solution: Jordan reversed the process. Carbon dioxide and water go in, and sugar and oxygen come out.
hint: Compare what goes in with what comes out.

text: Grass makes sugar using sunlight. When a grasshopper eats the grass, which product carries the energy it gets?
solution: The sugar a producer makes is its food and holds the energy from sunlight. That food energy passes to the grasshopper.
hint: Which product is the producer’s food?

text: What is a consumer?
answers: An organism that eats other organisms for energy
An organism that makes food from sunlight
An organism that never needs energy
solution: The lesson says consumers cannot use the Sun’s energy to make food, so they consume, or eat, other organisms.
hint: To “consume” means to eat.

text: Why is a bald eagle a consumer?
answers: It cannot use the Sun’s energy to make food, so it eats other organisms
It makes sugar in its feathers
It builds a nest out of sticks
It lives high up in a tree
solution: A bald eagle cannot make food from sunlight. It must eat other organisms for energy, which makes it a consumer.
hint: Ask how the eagle gets its energy.

text: The lesson’s example of a consumer that eats producers is the...
solution: The lesson says a consumer, such as the deer, may eat producers.
hint: Which animal eats plants?

text: The bald eagle is the lesson’s example of a consumer that eats...
solution: The lesson says some consumers, such as the bald eagle, may eat other consumers.
hint: Eagles hunt animals, not plants.

text: A bald eagle builds its nest from sticks. Does that make it a producer?
answers: No. It still gets its energy by eating other organisms
Yes, because sticks come from trees
Yes, because its nest is in the sunlight
No, because eagles do not need energy
solution: Using sticks to build a nest has nothing to do with food energy. The eagle cannot make food from sunlight, so it is a consumer.
hint: Producers are defined by how they get energy, not by what they build.

text: Which of these organisms is a consumer?
solution: A mouse eats other organisms, such as grasshoppers, for energy. Grass, lettuce, and cabbage are producers.
hint: Find the one that has to eat.

text: What is the main difference between a producer and a consumer?
answers: A producer makes food from sunlight; a consumer eats other organisms
A producer is always bigger than a consumer
A consumer makes food from sunlight; a producer eats
solution: Producers get energy directly from the Sun by making food. Consumers must eat other organisms to get energy.
hint: Compare how each one gets its energy.

text: A caterpillar munches on living leaves all day. Which statement is true?
answers: It is a consumer that eats a producer
It is a producer because it is green
It is a decomposer because it eats leaves
It gets energy directly from sunlight
solution: The caterpillar eats living leaves for energy, so it is a consumer eating a producer. Decomposers eat dead organisms.
hint: Is the caterpillar making food or eating it?

text: Grasshoppers eat grass, mice eat grasshoppers, and snakes eat mice. Which of these are consumers?
answers: The grasshopper, the mouse, and the snake
solution: All three animals eat other organisms for energy, so all three are consumers. Only the grass is a producer.
hint: Check each animal: does it eat something?

text: A student sitting in the sun says, “I’m getting my food energy right now!” Why is that wrong?
answers: People are consumers and cannot use sunlight to make food
People are producers, but only at noon
solution: Sunlight may warm you, but people cannot make food from it. As consumers, we get food energy by eating other organisms.
hint: Are people producers or consumers?

text: The graphic organizer says animals are called consumers because...
answers: They eat plants or other animals
They break down only dead matter
They get energy directly from the Sun
solution: The organizer says animals get energy from plants or other animals, so they are called consumers.
hint: “Consume” means to eat.

text: In grass → cow → humans, which organisms are consumers?
solution: The cow eats grass and humans eat the cow, so both are consumers. Grass is the producer.
hint: Which organisms must eat to get energy?

text: What do you call a consumer that eats only plants?
solution: The lesson says consumers that eat only plants are called herbivores.
hint: “Herb” is a clue about plants.

text: What do you call a consumer that eats only animals?
solution: The lesson says consumers that eat only animals are called carnivores.
hint: The word part “carn-” means meat.

text: What do you call a consumer that eats both plants and animals?
solution: The lesson says a consumer that eats both plants and animals is called an omnivore.
hint: The word part “omni-” means all.

text: A deer eats grass, leaves, and twigs. How should it be classified?
solution: Grass, leaves, and twigs all come from plants, so a deer that eats only plants is a herbivore.
hint: Are all of these foods plants, animals, or both?

text: A bald eagle catches fish and other animals. How should it be classified?
solution: An eagle that eats only animals is a carnivore.
hint: Does the eagle eat any plants?

text: Someone eats a hamburger with lettuce and tomato. Based on this meal, what are they?
solution: The beef came from an animal, and the lettuce and tomato came from plants. Eating both makes the person an omnivore.
hint: Sort each part of the meal into plant or animal.

text: A grasshopper eats only grass. Which word describes it?
solution: Grass is a plant, and a consumer that eats only plants is a herbivore.
hint: Grass is a plant, not an animal.

text: A family eats bacon and eggs for breakfast and a salad for lunch. What does this menu suggest about them?
solution: Bacon and eggs come from animals, and salad comes from plants. Eating both makes them omnivores.
hint: Check whether the meals include plants, animals, or both.

text: Sam says, “Snakes are omnivores because they live in the grass.” What is the best correction?
answers: Where an animal lives doesn’t decide its group; a snake that eats only animals is a carnivore
He is correct; living in grass makes an animal an omnivore
Snakes are herbivores because grass is nearby
solution: The groups depend on what a consumer eats, not where it lives. The snake in the lesson eats mice, so it is a carnivore.
hint: Ask what the snake eats, not where it lives.

text: A bear eats berries, roots, and fish. Why is “carnivore” the wrong label?
answers: It eats plants too, so it is an omnivore
It eats no animals at all
solution: Berries and roots are plants and fish are animals. An animal that eats both is an omnivore, not a carnivore.
hint: Does the bear eat only animals?

text: In the class food web, the bee and the deer were listed as...
solution: The class listed the bee and the deer as herbivores because they eat only plants or plant parts.
hint: Bees visit flowers; deer eat plants.

text: Which group from the class food web was listed as carnivores?
answers: Wolf, eagle, frog, owl, and snake
solution: The class listed the wolf, eagle, frog, owl, and snake as carnivores: consumers that eat only animals.
hint: Find the animals that hunt other animals.

text: The class listed the bear and the turtle as omnivores. What does that tell you about their diets?
answers: They eat both plants and animals
solution: An omnivore eats both plants and animals.
hint: Recall what “omni-” means.

text: What do decomposers eat?
solution: The lesson says decomposers eat only dead organisms.
hint: Think about the rotting log in the lesson.

text: Which group is made up of decomposers?
solution: The lesson names mushrooms, other fungi, and bacteria as decomposers.
hint: Which group breaks down dead things?

text: The lesson calls decomposers a special group of which kind of organism?
solution: Decomposers are a special group of consumers. They cannot make food from sunlight, so they eat dead organisms.
hint: Do decomposers make their own food or eat?

text: What do decomposers return to the food web?
solution: Decomposers break down the nutrients in dead organisms and return them to the food web.
hint: What is left in a dead organism that living things can use again?

text: A tree dies in a forest. According to the lesson, what happens next?
answers: Bacteria and fungi break it down and return its nutrients to the soil
solution: In the lesson’s example, bacteria and fungi consume the dead tree and return its nutrients to the soil.
hint: Which organisms eat dead things?

text: After fungi break down a dead tree, how does the forest grass benefit?
answers: It absorbs the returned nutrients and uses them to grow
It gets sunlight from the fungi
solution: The lesson says the grass absorbs the nutrients that decomposers returned to the soil and uses them to grow.
hint: Follow the nutrients from the tree to the soil to the grass.

text: In the lesson’s food chain diagram, which organisms break down dead materials left behind?
solution: The lesson says any dead materials left behind in the grass-to-hawk example are broken down by the mushrooms.
hint: Look for the decomposers in the picture.

text: Mushrooms are growing on a rotting log. What are they doing?
answers: Breaking down the dead wood and getting energy from it
Making food from sunlight like lettuce
Turning the log back into a living tree
solution: Mushrooms are decomposers. They eat the dead log, break it down, and return nutrients to the soil.
hint: Is the log living or dead?

text: A dead mouse and a fallen leaf are on the forest floor. Which can decomposers break down?
answers: Both the mouse and the leaf
solution: Decomposers may eat dead producers or dead consumers, so they can break down both the leaf and the mouse.
hint: Are both of these dead organisms?

text: If a forest had no decomposers, what problem would develop?
answers: Dead organisms would pile up, and their nutrients would not return to the soil
solution: Without decomposers, dead organisms would not be broken down, and plants would lose the nutrients that are normally returned to the soil.
hint: Think about what decomposers usually do for the soil.

text: According to the graphic organizer, what do decomposers such as bacteria return to the soil?
answers: Some of the matter from dead plants and animals
solution: The organizer says decomposers such as bacteria break down dead plants and animals and return some matter to the soil.
hint: What is left after a dead organism breaks down?

text: Which path of nutrients does the Decomposition Race reflection describe?
answers: Soil → plant → animal → back to the soil after decomposition
solution: The reflection says nutrients go from the soil to a plant, possibly to an animal that eats the plant, and back to the soil when the plant or animal dies and decomposes.
hint: Follow nutrients in a loop that ends where it started.

text: In the class food web, how were earthworms classified?
solution: The class listed earthworms, mushrooms, and bacteria together as detritivores and decomposers.
hint: Earthworms eat dead material in the soil.

text: What do detritivores, such as earthworms, do to dead material?
answers: Eat it and break it into smaller pieces
Turn it back into a living plant
Hunt it while it is still alive
solution: The CER explains that detritivores break the apple into smaller parts, which helps decomposers finish breaking it down.
hint: Think about what the worms did to the apple.

text: Why did breaking the apple into smaller parts help it decompose faster?
answers: Bacteria could decompose the smaller parts more quickly
The smaller parts got more sunlight and grew
The smaller parts turned into worms
solution: The CER reasoning says detritivores break the apple into smaller parts, allowing the bacteria to decompose the parts more quickly.
hint: Smaller pieces give decomposers more to work on at once.

text: In the CER, the earthworms are called detritivores. What are the bacteria called?
solution: The reasoning says worms are detritivores and bacteria are decomposers.
hint: Bacteria break down dead matter into tiny bits.

text: Mold grew on the apples in the Decomposition Race. What kind of organism is mold?
answers: A fungus that acts as a decomposer
A producer that makes food from sunlight
A herbivore that eats living plants
solution: Mold is a fungus. Fungi are decomposers, so mold on the apple is evidence that decomposition was happening.
hint: The lesson names fungi as decomposers.

text: Which three organisms from the class food web were listed as detritivores and decomposers?
solution: Earthworms, mushrooms, and bacteria all break down dead organisms. The class listed them together.
hint: Find the organisms that work on dead material.

text: How do earthworms and bacteria work together on a dead apple?
answers: Worms break it into smaller parts, and bacteria decompose those parts
Bacteria make the apple, and worms eat the bacteria
Worms make food from sunlight for the bacteria
They compete, so the apple never decays
solution: Detritivores like earthworms break material into smaller pieces. Decomposers like bacteria then break those pieces down more quickly.
hint: Who does the chopping, and who finishes the job?

text: In the class food web, arrows from many organisms lead to the earthworms, mushrooms, and bacteria. Why?
answers: They get energy from dead organisms of every kind
They give energy to the Sun
solution: When any plant or animal dies, detritivores and decomposers break it down, so arrows lead to them from many organisms.
hint: What happens to every organism eventually?

text: Ty says, “Earthworms are producers because they live in the soil.” What is the best correction?
answers: Earthworms eat dead material; living in soil does not make something a producer
He is right; anything in soil is a producer
Earthworms make food from sunlight underground
Earthworms are carnivores that hunt plants
solution: Producers make their own food using the Sun’s energy. Earthworms eat dead material, so they are detritivores.
hint: Ask how earthworms get their energy.

text: According to the reflection, what is happening to the decomposing apple?
answers: It is decomposing and will eventually return to the soil
It is disappearing completely, with nothing left
It is growing into a new apple right away
solution: The reflection says the apple is decomposing and will eventually return to the soil.
hint: Where does decomposing matter end up?

text: The apple with earthworms was mostly gone. What does the CER say happened to its matter?
answers: It was moved or changed, not destroyed
The worms turned it into new apples
solution: The evidence says the matter was moved or changed. Decomposition breaks material down and returns it to the soil; matter does not just disappear.
hint: Matter can change form or location.

text: According to the reflection, why is decomposition good for the environment?
answers: Dead things do not pile up, and their nutrients help new plants grow
It creates more dead plants and animals
It keeps nutrients locked away from plants
solution: Without decomposition, dead plants and animals would pile up. Decomposers return matter and nutrients to the soil, where they help new plants grow.
hint: Think about both the dead material and the soil.

text: What was the driving question of the Decomposition Race?
answers: What factors affect the decomposition process?
How much water can soil hold?
solution: The investigation’s driving question was “What factors affect the decomposition process?”
hint: The question is about what changes how decomposition happens.

text: What was the one planned difference between the two containers?
answers: One container had earthworms; the other did not
One had soil; the other had none
One had apple; the other had none
One got water; the other got none
solution: Both containers got soil, moist paper strips, and half an apple. Only one got earthworms.
hint: Read procedure step 5.

text: Why did both containers get the same soil, moistened paper strips, and half of the same apple?
answers: So earthworms were the only planned difference, making the test fair
So the containers would look nice
To give the worms more room
solution: Keeping everything else the same means any difference in decomposition can be linked to the earthworms.
hint: In a fair test, how many things should you change on purpose?

text: How much soil went into each container?
solution: Procedure step 1 says to put 500 mL of soil into each container. The group’s 1,000 mL of soil was split between the two.
hint: The group had 1,000 mL to share between two containers.

text: How long did students observe the containers?
solution: Procedure step 6 says to make daily observations for 2–3 weeks and record them in the data table.
hint: Decomposition takes time. Check step 6.

text: By Week 3, how did the apple with worms compare with the apple without worms?
answers: It was mushy with many holes and falling apart
It looked just as it did on the first day
It had turned back into a whole apple
solution: The data table shows the apple with worms became mushy with many holes and was falling apart. The apple without worms was dark and mushy but still in one piece.
hint: Look at the Week 3 “Worms” column.

text: What claim does the Decomposition Race CER make?
answers: Earthworms and bacteria helped break down the apple
solution: The claim is that the earthworms and bacteria helped break down the apple.
hint: A claim answers the prompt in one sentence.

text: Which observation is evidence for the claim that earthworms helped break down the apple?
answers: The apple with worms decomposed more than the apple without worms
The apple was cut in half
solution: Evidence is an observation that supports the claim. Comparing the two apples shows more decomposition with worms. The other choices describe the setup.
hint: Evidence comes from the results, not the materials list.

text: The apple without worms still turned dark and mushy. What best explains this?
answers: Decomposers like bacteria and mold were still breaking it down, just more slowly
The apple was making food from sunlight
solution: Decomposers such as bacteria and mold work even without worms. The worms sped decomposition up by breaking the apple into smaller parts.
hint: Worms help, but are they the only decomposers?

text: In this system, how did living things and nonliving matter interact?
answers: Earthworms helped break down the apple and return nutrients to the soil
The apple made food for the soil from sunlight
solution: The reflection says the living earthworms helped break down the apple and return nutrients (matter) back to the soil.
hint: Connect the worms to the soil.

text: Which of these did the reflection list as a factor that affects decomposition?
solution: The reflection lists factors such as what is eating the material, how much time passes, the soil, and oxygen.
hint: Choose something that could really change how decomposers work.

text: In a claim–evidence–reasoning explanation, what does the reasoning do?
answers: Uses science ideas to explain why the evidence supports the claim
Repeats the claim in different words
Gives an opinion with no science
solution: In the CER, the reasoning uses science ideas (detritivores and decomposers) to explain why the evidence supports the claim.
hint: Reasoning connects evidence to the claim.
